newsitem.title: USA: Business inventories up slightly in November.
newsitem.headline: Business inventories up slightly in November.

text.p: Stocks of unsold goods at businesses barely rose in November as companies prepared warily for Christmas, the Commerce Department said Wednesday.
Total business inventories edged up only 0.1 percent in November to a seasonally adjusted $1.01 trillion after an 0.5 percent rise in October, the department said.

Analysts said lean inventories and record low stock-to-sales ratios as 1996 was ending may clear the way for stronger production in the current first quarter by stimulating investment to rebuild stocks.
The key change during November occurred at retailers, where inventories shrank 0.4 percent to $314.05 billion after a 0.8 percent October increase.
"Inventories did not expand robustly," said economist Kevin Harris of MCM Moneywatch in New York. "There was some caution ahead of Christmas, obviously."

The caution apparently was warranted. On Tuesday, the Commerce Department reported December retail sales increased a relatively modest 0.6 percent and were up for all of 1996 by just 5.3 percent from 1995.

Merchants previously said Christmas sales, though stronger than a year earlier, were not as robust as anticipated. Expectations had been high because jobs were plentiful and incomes grew throughout most of 1996 and the stock market was booming.
Business sales were up in November by 0.6 percent to $729.83 billion, a third consecutive monthly increase after a 0.4 percent rise in October.

That left the stock-to-sales ratio, which measures how long it would take to clear out inventories at the current sales pace, at a record low 1.39 months in November, the same as in September and October. It was the lowest ratio since the Commerce Department began keeping records in 1982.
Said Harris of MCM, "1.39 months is reasonably tight. Certainly it is not a level that poses a threat to future production rates."
The small drop in November retail inventories was the first decline in eight months, since they fell 0.9 percent in March. Most of the drop occurred at automobile dealers and furniture stores.

By contrast, manufacturers' inventories rose 0.4 percent in November to $439.89 billion after a 0.3 percent October rise, while wholesale inventories edged up 0.1 percent to $285.02 billion following a 0.3 percent October increase.
Though sales were not quite as robust as hoped for at Christmas, there was no suggestion the retail sector was suffering as it headed into the holiday sales season.
To the contrary, profits were growing solidly.
Separately, the Commerce Department reported that after-tax profits of U.S. retailers rose to 2 cents out of each sales dollar during the third quarter from 1.7 cents in the third quarter.
Total profits were $4.84 billion after taxes, up from $3.95 billion in the second quarter and sharply above the $3.59 billion that retailers cleared a year earlier in the third quarter of 1995.
The profit estimate was based on quarterly financial reports from 547 retail corporations, each of which had assets of $50 million or more.
